name: Erlitou culture
title: The story of the Erlitou culture

text: About 3,700 years ago, the Erlitou culture grew up in the Yellow River valley of China.
Its main city, Erlitou, stood on the Yi River and grew to perhaps 24,000 people.
src: c. 1750 BCE: By radiocarbon dating the Erlitou culture begins / an early Bronze Age society and archaeological culture of the Yellow River valley
The city of Erlitou stood on the Yi River / The city peaked in Phase III, with perhaps 24,000 people

text: The land around the city had no copper, so the ore had to be brought from mountains farther away.
Tracks found near its palace are the oldest signs of wagons with wheels in China.
src: The Luoyang Plain has no copper, so ore had to be brought in, perhaps from the Zhongtiao Mountains of southern Shanxi
Tracks of vehicles near the palace are the earliest evidence of wheeled wagons in China

text: Erlitou was the first culture in China to make bronze on a large scale.
Its workers cast bronze in moulds to make tools, bells, weapons and special pots for ceremonies.
src: The Erlitou culture was the earliest large-scale bronze-producing culture in China
Its casters used a new section-mould process to make ritual vessels and other bronzes / tools, bells, weapons, distinctive animal-faced plaques and more than ten kinds of vessel

text: About 3,600 years ago a new culture, the Erligang, grew strong, and later Erlitou stopped making bronzes.
There is no sign of fire or war, but its palaces were left empty and the city became a village.
src: Its end came with the rise of the Erligang culture / around 1600 BCE a walled city was built at Yanshi / Production of bronzes and other elite goods at Erlitou stopped at the end of Phase IV
There is no evidence of destruction by fire or war, but during the Upper Erligang phase (1450–1300 BCE) all the palaces were abandoned and Erlitou was reduced to a village of 30 ha

text: Much later, old books told of an early line of kings called the Xia.
Many scholars think Erlitou was a Xia city, but others say no writing has been found to prove it.
src: Those accounts, at first oral, were written down much later, in the Bamboo Annals (c. 300 BCE) and the Records of the Grand Historian / the capitals of the Xia and Shang dynasties

many scholars, especially in China, see it as the Xia’s material remains and Erlitou as its capital / some Western scholars call this premature, since no contemporary writing has been found to prove the link

text: Among its finds are the oldest bronze ding found in China, a kind of pot for ceremonies.
Today more than 2,000 objects from Erlitou are shown in a museum in Luoyang.
src: Erlitou monopolised the making of ritual bronze vessels, including the earliest ding found in China
The Erlitou Site Museum of the Xia Capital, with more than 2,000 objects from the site, opens in Luoyang
